text: Lygia Pape (7 April 1927 – 3 May 2004) was a Brazilian visual artist, sculptor, engraver, and filmmaker who played a key role in the Concrete movement and later co-founded the Neo-Concrete Movement in Brazil during the 1950s and 1960s. Born in Nova Friburgo, Brazil, she studied philosophy at the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFTJ) and received informal training in fine arts, studying with Fayga Ostrower at the Museum of Modern Art, Rio de Janeiro. At age 20, she joined the Concrete art movement, a term coined by Dutch artist Theo van Doesburg in 1930. In the 1950s, she created the Tecelares Series, woodblock prints characterized by precise geometric forms, minimalism, and the use of black ink on rice paper, with thin lines that reveal the white paper beneath. These works employed a weaving metaphor to connect with Brazil’s traditional and indigenous cultures, where geometry expressed collective identity rather than industrialization. The 1959 Tecelares print, Sem Título [Untitled], features parallel lines disrupted by non-orthogonal lines, creating the illusion of separate planes and space. Despite its Concrete origins, the work shows handmade qualities—slight line variations and ink feathering—indicating a human touch and marking a transition into Neo-Concrete art. The 1960 version is even more organic, with visible wood grain and subtle diagonal lines that create movement, opposing the mechanistic ideals of Concrete art. In 1952, at age 25, Pape met Hélio Oiticica, Ivan Serpa, and Aluísio Carvão, forming the Grupo Frente, which rejected traditional Brazilian painting and explored abstract and geometric forms. The group held exhibitions in 1954 at Ibeu Gallery and in 1955 at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio, emphasizing non-traditional use of line, form, and color. A debate between Grupo Ruptura and Grupo Frente over the rigidity of geometric abstraction inspired Pape and others to launch the Neo-Concrete Movement in 1959. Pape signed the Neo-Concrete Manifesto alongside Lygia Clark and Hélio Oiticica, emphasizing invention and a desire to discover new ways of knowing the world through art. During this period, she explored the idea of “living the body,” creating multi-sensorial experiences. Her work Livro da Criação [Book of Creation] consists of sixteen unbound cardboard pages, each depicting moments in the creation of the world, designed for phenomenological engagement where each reader interprets it differently. In the 1960s and 1970s, she produced videos and installations critical of the Brazilian dictatorship, with more subtle metaphors from the 1980s onward. Her 1975 film Eat Me features slow-motion sensual movements of mouths, interpreted as implicating gender and sexuality, and is seen as objectifying women despite Pape’s insistence it is not a thesis. In 1967, the installation O Ovo involved participants crawling into a wooden cube covered in plastic film and pushing through it to simulate birth. From 1972 to 1985, Pape taught semiotics at the School of Architecture at the Universidade Santa Úrsula in Rio de Janeiro, becoming a professor at the School of Fine Arts of the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro in 1983. She earned a master’s degree in philosophy from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro in 1980 and introduced her students to the informal architecture of Rio’s favelas, especially Maré. In 1981, she received a Guggenheim Fellowship. Her first retrospective was in 2000, focusing on her print practice, which she viewed as a generative source of her artistic career. Ttéias (1979) is emblematic of her process; conceived in 1979 and fully realized in the 1990s, it began with experiments in arranging metallic strings at Parque Lage Gardens in Rio. The word "Ttéias" is a pun on "teia" (web) and "teteia" (a person or thing of grace), consisting of semi-transparent prisms made from gold thread, allowing immersive, interpretive experiences. Pape’s work is held in the Museum of Modern Art, the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, and the Tate. It was included in the 2021 exhibition Women in Abstraction at the Centre Pompidou. In 2025/2026, she received her first solo exhibition in France, Weaving Space, at the Pinault Collection, Bourse de Commerce. Pape did not work with a commercial gallery until later in life. Projeto Lygia Pape, established by her before her death in 2004 and managed by her daughter Paula Pape, was involved in a 2017 U.S. lawsuit against LG Electronics, several mobile phone vendors, and Getty Images Korea for copyright infringement of her 2003 sculpture TtEia 1, C, used in packaging and advertising for the K20 V mobile phone. Pape died on 3 May 2004 in Rio de Janeiro at the age of 77.
